newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FOCUS-Sri Lanka rubber production seen recovering.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sri Lanka rubber production seen recovering.

text.p: Increased use of high-yielding clones and dry weather will boost Sri Lanka's rubber production this year, a top researcher forecast on Tuesday.
"We forecast production this year will be 118,000 tonnes, up from 108,000 tonnes in 1995," said Keerthi Tillekeratne, director of the government Rubber Research Institute (RRI).

"The population of high-yielding clones is increasing along with the use of rain-guards," he told Reuters. "Also, we had dry weather in the first six months of the year which helped increase production."
The Indian Ocean island now accounts for just two percent of the world's natural rubber output, having slipped from the world's fourth biggest rubber producer to eighth in 25 years.

Rubber production is forecast to rise to 120,000 tonnes in 1997, 122,000 tonnes in 1988 and reach 126,000 tonnes by 2000, Tillekeratne said. This compares with a record output of 155,000 tonnes in 1978.

Rubber exports this year are expected to be around 69,000 tonnes, about the same as last year, because of increasing domestic consumption which now takes up about 38 percent of the crop, Tillekeratne said.
Domestic consumption was growing with new glove, tyre and other rubber-based industries being set up, he said.
Earnings from rubber exports rose sharply to 5.7 billion rupees ($102 million) last year from 1994's 3.6 billion rupees ($64 million), a spokesman for the Rubber Development Department said.
Tillekeratne also said the government was considering introducing new laws to stop the alarming decline in the acreage under rubber.
"The acreage under rubber is now declining at the rate of 3,000 hectares (7,400 acres) a year, mainly because of village expansion and increasing urbanisation as the population rises," he said.
"Therefore, from the available small acreage we must try to raise productivity by going for high-yielding clones and the use of rain-guards," he added.
The Rubber Development Department spokesman said the acreage under rubber had fallen to around 161,479 hectares (399,019 acres) from 171,152 hectares (422,921 acres) in the early 1980s.
Tillekeratne said up to 50 percent of production was sometimes lost due to rain which prevented tapping.

"Our yields have gone down to a national average of about 870 kg per hectare per year," he said. "Therefore, we are asking producers to somehow use rain-guards. In Kerala (southern India) their yield is around 1,440 kg/hectare per year because of the use of rain-guards.
"Also, we're not maintaining the stand -- the number of trees per acre which is very poor," he added. "In India it is extremely well-maintained."
China is the biggest buyer of Sri Lanka's rubber. Other big buyers of sheet rubber are India, Pakistan and Russia while the United Kingdom, Canada and Japan are the main buyers of crepe.
